summary: Describes protocol options for carrying objects protected by the Cryptographic Message Syntax and S/MIME version 3.1 across an X.400 message transfer system. It covers how those secured objects are conveyed in X.400 messages.

eli5.summary: If a locked box must ride a different delivery service, this document explains how to put it on the truck so it arrives sealed.

subtitle: How to carry S/MIME-protected objects inside native X.400 messages, and how to label them.

tldr.problem: S/MIME objects protected with CMS can travel over many mail systems, but X.400 has no MIME typing and needs agreed rules for where the object goes and how its kind is signalled.
tldr.mechanism: The CMS object is placed in the content field of the X.400 message, the P1 envelope content-type is set to a given OID, and Encoded Information Type (EIT) OIDs take the place of the MIME smime-type parameter.
tldr.outcome: Native X.400 systems can exchange signed and encrypted S/MIME messages interoperably, though gateways that expect IPMS cannot do anything with them.

today: RFC 3855 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works with RFC 3854, which defines how to protect the X.400 content itself.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
CMS objects and S/MIME messages can be carried by many email systems. RFC 3855 defines the options and values needed to transport S/MIME messages interoperably over an X.400 system, using CMS objects as the message content in a native X.400 environment.

That choice has a consequence: gateways or other functions that expect to deal with IPMS, such as those in RFC 2156 (MIXER) and RFC 2157, cannot do anything with these messages. Gateway services between X.400 and SMTP are out of scope. A goal is to keep backward compatibility, if possible, with existing X.400 implementations that use S/MIME v3.1 wrappers.
sections.eli5: It explains how to send sealed letters on the old mail truck. The people who sort other kinds of mail will not be able to open these letters.

sections.title: The X.400 Message Structure
sections.content:
An X.400 message has an envelope and a content. The envelope identifies the originator and recipients, records how the message has been conveyed, and characterizes the content. The content is what the originating User Agent wants delivered. The Message Transfer System (MTS) neither examines nor modifies the content, except for conversion, and conversion does not apply here because it is incompatible with CMS protection.

The envelope carries a content type, an ASN.1 OID or integer that says what the content is. Some content types, such as the Interpersonal Messaging System (IPMS), split content into heading elements and body parts, each identified by a body part type.
sections.eli5: A letter has an outside with addresses and a note about what is inside, and the inside part. The mail carriers should only read the outside.

sections.title: Carrying S/MIME as X.400 Content
sections.content:
The preferred way is to convey the CMS object as the X.400 message content. Implementations MUST include the CMS object in the content field of the X.400 message. This works whatever mail content was encapsulated.

The content-type field of the P1 envelope then depends on whether an outer MIME wrapper covers the CMS object:

  • With an outer MIME wrapper, it MUST be set to id-data.
  • Without one, it MUST be set to id-ct-contentInfo.

A plaintext MIME object sent in X.400 is also best conveyed as the message content, with the P1 content-type set to id-data.

On transfer encoding, the optional outer MIME wrapper that supports 7-bit transport is not required for X.400 and generally SHOULD NOT be applied in a homogeneous X.400 environment, though heterogeneous mail systems or other factors MAY require it.
sections.eli5: The sealed letter goes straight into the content part of the delivery, and the outside label says which kind of wrapping it has.

sections.title: Forwarding in IPMS Body Parts
sections.content:
Implementations generally SHOULD NOT embed CMS objects in X.400 body parts. The notable exception is forwarding. When a CMS object is forwarded as part of a message forwarding function, implementations MUST use the content-body-part defined in X.400.

The implementation MUST copy the CMS object into the Content field of that body part. The direct-reference field MUST carry the OID formed by joining id-et-content to id-ct-contentInfo, which for any CMS object gives the DATA component the identifier { 2 6 1 4 17 1 2 840 113549 1 9 16 1 6 }. The ForwardedContentParameters are optional. In this case the P1 envelope content-type is set to the value for the forwarding content, such as integer 22 for IPMS.
sections.eli5: Normally the sealed letter rides on its own. Only when someone passes the letter along inside another letter does it go in a special pocket.

sections.title: Labelling Messages with Encoded Information Types
sections.content:
In S/MIME the smime-type parameter tells a receiver what protection was applied. X.400 has no MIME typing, so the same meaning is conveyed with Encoded Information Types (EITs) in the original-encoded-information-types field of the envelope. Each EIT is an OID under id-eit.

Sending agents SHOULD include the appropriate S/MIME EIT OID. Receiving agents SHOULD recognize them and process the message according to local procedures. New EIT values should correspond one-to-one to assigned smime-type values, and may coexist with other EIT values describing the protected content.

Two of the types connect to RFC 3854: the enveloped X.400 and signed X.400 types are for X.400 content protected as that RFC describes. The certs-only type is a single SignedData with no eContent and an empty signerInfos field, used to move certificates and CRLs.
sections.eli5: On the outside of the box you write what kind of seal is inside, using a code from an agreed list.

sections.title: Interaction with X.400 Services
sections.content:
Some X.400 services can interact badly with SignedData and EnvelopedData, so the RFC advises care.

  • Conversion: the Conversion Prohibition service SHOULD be selected.
  • Redirection: forms include Originator Requested Alternate Recipient (ORAR), alternate recipient assignment and redirection of incoming messages. An EnvelopedData object needs a RecipientInfo for each recipient and alternate recipient, and one for the originator is good practice in case the MTS returns the whole message. With ORAR the originator SHOULD include a RecipientInfo for the alternate recipient.
  • Distribution lists: X.400 DLs are not generally security-aware and do not regenerate RecipientInfo elements for members. A security-aware mail list conforming to RFC 2634 is preferred, and the DL Expansion Prohibited service SHOULD be selected.
sections.eli5: Some mail helpers, like ones that forward letters or copy them to a whole list, cannot open locked boxes. So each person who should read the letter needs their own key slot, and the helpers should be told not to meddle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security concerns to the CMS or S/MIME models, and points to the security sections of the S/MIME Message Specification (RFC 3851), the Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME and CMS.
sections.eli5: It adds no new dangers. Read the older rulebooks for the usual ones.
